title: Peer into the crater lake at Poas Volcano
description: Entry is capped and must be booked online for a specific time slot - turn up without one and you're turned away at the gate. The lake is one of the most acidic on earth and the park closes within minutes if gas readings spike.

title: Swim beneath La Fortuna waterfall
description: 500 concrete steps down a cliff face to a 70m fall you can swim beneath, then the same 500 back up in tropical heat. The current at the base is stronger than it looks - stay inside the roped swimming area.

title: Hike to the turquoise water of Rio Celeste
description: The colour is pure chemistry, not paint or dye - an optical effect from particle size where two clear, colourless rivers of different mineral content meet. Swimming is banned to protect it, so bring a rain jacket instead of togs.

title: Stand in the moonscape crater of Irazu Volcano
description: The country's highest volcano, barren enough at the top to be nicknamed the moonscape. Arrive before 10am - cloud rolls in most days by late morning and the view of both oceans from the summit disappears.

title: Drive the Orosi Valley loop past coffee farms and colonial ruins
description: The country's oldest surviving church, coffee farms ringing a volcanic crater, and the Ujarras ruins half-swallowed by jungle since a flood destroyed the town in 1833 - an hour from the capital and largely ignored by it.

title: Raft the Pacuare River whitewater
description: Consistently rated one of the best whitewater runs on the planet, Class III-IV through a roadless gorge - some lodges along it can only be reached by raft, so the trip out is the only way home.

title: Glide above the canopy on the Braulio Carrillo aerial tram
description: A ski-lift-style gondola through primary rainforest canopy that no footpath could reach without cutting a scar through it - built by one of the biologists behind Iguazu's walkway system.

title: Follow cacao to chocolate at Tirimbina
description: Costa Rica exported cacao a century before coffee ever arrived. The tour crosses a hanging bridge over the Sarapiqui River and ends with a bar you helped roast - stains your hands and changes what you think chocolate is supposed to taste like.

title: Walk the mud pots and hot springs of Rincon de la Vieja
description: Bubbling sulphur pots, a hidden waterfall and natural hot springs inside an active volcano's national park. The summit trail closes for months at a stretch whenever activity rises - check before you build a trip around it.

title: Watch the olive ridley arribada at Ostional
description: Tens of thousands of turtles crawl ashore over two or three nights each lunar cycle, in numbers so dense that later arrivals dig up earlier nests. It's one of the few beaches on earth where locals are legally permitted to harvest a share of the eggs, which funds the patrols protecting the rest.

title: Surf Witch's Rock at Playa Naranjo
description: Reachable only by boat or a rough hour of 4WD track through Santa Rosa National Park, the wave that closed Endless Summer II is still one of the world's few great breaks with no beachfront development anywhere in sight.

title: Walk the crushed-shell sand of Playa Conchal
description: The sand here is crushed shell rather than quartz, which gives it a coarse sparkle underfoot and means it never gets uncomfortably hot at midday the way the beaches either side of it do.

title: Spot sloths on the trails of Manuel Antonio
description: The country's smallest national park and its most visited, packing sloths and squirrel monkeys onto trails that end at a beach once ranked among the best in the world by National Geographic. Book entry online - daily numbers are capped and it sells out in high season.

title: Dive Isla del Cano from Drake Bay
description: A biological reserve 20km offshore with the best visibility on the Pacific coast, and the usual jump-off point for exploring Corcovado without hiking in - Drake Bay itself still has no reliable road connection in wet season.

title: Walk the whale-tail sandbar at Marino Ballena
description: A sandbar shaped exactly like a whale's tail, walkable only at low tide, in a park that gets humpback whales from two different hemispheres migrating through in different halves of the year - one of the longest whale seasons anywhere on earth.

title: Learn to surf at Jaco
description: The closest real surf beach to San Jose, which makes it the easiest place in the country to learn - consistent beach breaks, boards for rent on every corner, and a two-hour drive instead of a flight.

title: Ride to the twin pools of Nauyaca Waterfalls
description: A two-tiered fall on private ranch land reached by horseback or 4WD, with a swimming pool at the base that locals still consider a well-kept alternative to the crowds at La Fortuna.

title: Walk the free reef trail at Cahuita
description: One of the only national parks in the country with no entry fee - it runs on donations instead. Sloths and howler monkeys hang over the beach trail, and the reef just offshore is the best snorkelling on the Caribbean side.

title: Watch the reef break at Salsa Brava
description: A wave that breaks hard over a shallow reef a few hundred metres offshore, named for how it 'slaps' surfers who misjudge it. Advanced only - the town's other breaks nearby are far more forgiving.

title: Explore the untouched coast of Gandoca-Manzanillo
description: The last stretch of undeveloped Caribbean coast in the country, where the road simply ends and a rainforest trail takes over - howler monkeys and sloths overhead, and manatees in the lagoons behind the beach.

title: Wander the balconies of Casco Viejo
description: Panama City's original quarter, built after pirates burned the first site to the ground in 1671. Restored blocks of French balconies and rooftop bars sit one street away from blocks still waiting their turn.

title: Tour a geisha coffee farm in Boquete
description: A cool-climate highland town growing some of the most expensive coffee on earth - geisha varietals from a single Boquete farm have sold at auction for over $100 a pound.

title: Climb Volcan Baru overnight for sunrise
description: Panama's only volcano and highest point, climbed through the night to crest 3,474m for sunrise - on a clear morning it's the one spot on earth where you can see both the Pacific and the Caribbean at once.

title: Canoe up the Chagres River to an Embera village
description: Reached by dugout canoe up the same river system that feeds the Panama Canal's fresh water, to a village that runs on solar power and still paints visitors with temporary jagua tattoos the way it always has.

title: Dive the sharks and rays of Coiba
description: A former penal colony left alone for decades because nobody but prisoners was allowed near it - now one of the last places in the eastern Pacific with real numbers of sharks and rays.

title: Walk the Spanish forts at Portobelo
description: Forts guarding the harbour where the silver of the entire Peruvian empire was loaded for Spain. Once a year a life-size Black Christ statue is carried through the streets by purple-robed devotees fulfilling vows.

title: Surf the point break at Santa Catalina
description: A fishing village with one of the best right-hand point breaks in Central America, and the usual launch point for boats into Coiba - most surfers only meant to stay a few days and are still there months later.

title: Island hop the Pearl Islands from Contadora
description: The pearl-fishing islands that reputedly supplied Spain's crown jewels, a 20-minute flight from the capital, with a swimmable beach on one side and whales passing close inshore on the other in season.

title: Wander the market inside the crater at El Valle de Anton
description: A town built inside the second-largest inhabited volcanic crater on earth, with a Sunday market and a golden frog now extinct in the wild almost everywhere else.

title: Get soaked at Las Tablas carnival
description: Panama's biggest carnival, split between two rival streets that douse each other and the crowd with water-cannon trucks every afternoon before the real parade starts at night.

title: Snorkel the Zapatillas Cays
description: Two uninhabited cays inside Bastimentos National Marine Park that look like a stock photo of a desert island, because they were used as one - a season of Survivor filmed here.

title: Bird Pipeline Road in Soberania
description: Held the world record for most bird species recorded in 24 hours for over three decades. A rutted track through old rainforest 40 minutes from a capital city, named for the historic pipeline it still runs alongside.

title: Enter the Darien wilderness with a Wounaan guide
description: One of the last true wildernesses in the Americas and the only gap in the Pan-American Highway, entered legally and safely only with an indigenous Wounaan or Embera guide arranged in advance - and unrelated to the migrant trail on the Colombian side.

title: Hike Indian Nose for sunrise over Lake Atitlan
description: Guides leave San Pedro by headlamp around 4am so you're on the ridge before first light - the profile the peak is named for only reads clearly from the water far below. Bring a jacket, it's genuinely cold at altitude before the sun clears the volcanoes.

title: Kayak the crater lake from San Pedro La Laguna
description: Lake Atitlan fills a volcanic caldera nearly 300 metres deep, and the water is glassy at dawn and choppy by early afternoon once the Xocomil wind picks up - paddle out before 11am or plan to fight a headwind home.

title: Watch natural dyes made at a San Juan weaving cooperative
description: Women's weaving cooperatives here still dye cotton with cochineal insects, indigo and avocado pits rather than synthetic dye, and demonstrate the whole process before you buy - a different pitch entirely to the market stalls in Panajachel.

title: Trek multiple days through jungle to El Mirador's pyramids
description: No road reaches it - the only ways in are a five-day round-trip hike or a helicopter charter, to a pyramid complex larger than anything at Tikal that almost nobody visiting Guatemala this year will ever see. Mule-supported camping trips need booking weeks ahead in dry season.

title: Watch sunset from Yaxha's temple over the lagoon
description: Smaller and far quieter than Tikal, with a temple platform looking over Laguna Yaxha where howler monkeys start calling right as the sun drops - a Survivor season filmed its closing scenes here, but most afternoons it's nearly empty.

title: Bargain the stalls at Chichicastenango market
description: One of the largest indigenous markets in the Americas, but it only reaches full size on Thursdays and Sundays - arrive on any other day and half the plaza is empty stalls. Photographing the syncretic rituals on the church steps out front without asking causes real offence.

title: Tour a working coffee finca outside Antigua
description: Guatemala's volcanic soil and altitude produce some of the world's most prized arabica, and the harvest tours run only from November through February - visit outside that window and there are no cherries left on the trees to see picked.

title: Roast marshmallows on hot lava rock at Pacaya
description: The most active and most climbed volcano in the country, close enough to the capital for a half-day trip - the hardened black rock near the summit stays warm enough underfoot to toast a marshmallow on a stick, no fire required.

title: Watch the bat exodus from Lanquin's caves at dusk
description: A river runs straight through the cave mouth, lit for a stretch by hanging bulbs before the path turns to candlelight only. Time it for dusk and hundreds of thousands of bats stream out overhead on their way to feed.

title: Hike to the perfectly round jungle lake at Laguna Lachua
description: A near-perfect circle of water inside dense rainforest, reached by a 4km trail from the ranger station with no road access and no development anywhere on the shore. Park-run cabins are the only place to stay and need booking directly with the reserve.

title: Boat through the limestone gorge of Rio Dulce
description: The river narrows into a canyon of hanging jungle and hot sulphur springs bubbling straight out of the cliff face at Aguas Calientes, on the same run boats take between Livingston and the Rio Dulce town bridge.

title: Eat tapado in the Garifuna town of Livingston
description: Reachable only by boat, never by road, with a Garifuna culture, language and coconut-milk seafood stew found nowhere else in the country. Punta drumming on the beach after dark is unannounced and just happens.

title: Swim beneath a hot waterfall at Finca El Paraiso
description: A thermal river drops straight into a cool jungle pool, so the temperature shifts by the metre depending on how close you swim to the falls. Go on a weekday morning - weekend tour buses from Rio Dulce crowd the pool by early afternoon.

title: Release baby turtles into the surf at Monterrico
description: A black volcanic-sand beach where a community hatchery collects eggs poached elsewhere and lets visitors release the hatchlings at sunset. The hatchery survives almost entirely on the small per-turtle release donation.

title: Summit Tajumulco, the highest point in Central America
description: Most groups camp partway up and push for the 4,220m summit before dawn, above the cloud line and cold enough most nights to frost the tents. On a clear morning both the Pacific coast and Mexico's volcanoes are visible at once.

title: Go slow on car-free Caye Caulker
description: The island's official motto is literally 'Go Slow', and it's enforced - golf carts and bikes only, no rental cars, and the one paved road out to the Split swimming hole takes about fifteen minutes to walk end to end.

title: Snorkel with nurse sharks at Shark Ray Alley
description: A shallow sandbar inside Hol Chan Marine Reserve where fishermen once cleaned their catch, which trained generations of nurse sharks and southern stingrays to associate boats with food - they still circle within arm's reach of every snorkel tour.

title: Climb El Castillo at Xunantunich
description: A hand-cranked cable ferry is still the only way across the Mopan River to reach it - no bridge, so the site closes when the ferry does at 4pm. The frieze on El Castillo's upper section is a rare surviving example of Maya stucco decoration.

title: Climb Caana, still the tallest building in Belize, at Caracol
description: Deep in the Chiquibul forest near the Guatemalan border, reached by a rough road that requires a police-escorted convoy at set times. Once the largest Maya city in the region, bigger than Tikal at its peak, and rarely more than a handful of other visitors on site.

title: Float an inner tube through Nohoch Che'en's cave river
description: An underground river tour by tube and headlamp through limestone caverns the Maya once used for ceremonies. The water stays a near-constant temperature all year, so the caves draw almost as many visitors in wet season as dry.

title: Swim the granite pools of Rio On in Mountain Pine Ridge
description: A forest reserve of pine ridges rather than the jungle found everywhere else in the country, where the Rio On carves a run of granite boulders into natural waterslides and swimming pools. Bring your own food - there's nothing for sale inside the reserve.

title: Walk jaguar trails in Cockscomb Basin
description: The world's first wildlife sanctuary created specifically to protect jaguars, though camera traps rather than luck are the realistic way to know one is nearby. The night walk instead reliably turns up kinkajous, tarantulas and red-eyed tree frogs.

title: Learn Garifuna drumming in Hopkins village
description: A Garifuna fishing village where drum schools run lessons on hand-carved mahogany drums most afternoons. Turn up at the right guesthouse on a Saturday night and the lesson turns into an actual community jam session.

title: Sail the reef out of Placencia
description: A 26km sand peninsula reached by a road so narrow the airstrip crosses it, with a sidewalk locally billed as the narrowest street in the world. Day-sail trips out to the cayes leave right from the main village dock.

title: Boat up the New River to Lamanai's ruins
description: The hour-long river approach past crocodiles and howler monkeys is as much the point as the ruins themselves. One of the few Maya sites occupied through the Spanish and British colonial periods, which is why its name means 'submerged crocodile' rather than a modern archaeologist's label.

title: Meet rescued jaguars and tapirs at the Belize Zoo
description: Built entirely around animals that couldn't be released after film shoots or rescue - almost every resident is native to Belize. The night tour is the only reliable way to see the jaguars actually awake and active.

title: Wander the colonial streets of Granada
description: Nicaragua's oldest colonial city, founded in 1524 and repeatedly burned by pirates and filibusters since - the mustard-yellow cathedral you see today is a 20th-century rebuild, not the original. Climb the bell tower for the best rooftop view over the red-tiled centre.

title: Boat through the 365 Isletas de Granada
description: A scatter of small islands formed when Mombacho volcano partially collapsed centuries ago, now home to everything from egret colonies to a private fort and a restaurant reachable only by kayak. Locals say there's one islet for every day of the year, though nobody has ever agreed on the exact count.

title: Walk the cloud forest crater trail on Mombacho Volcano
description: A 4WD truck hauls you up the steep access road since the park limits vehicle numbers to protect the trail, then a short walk circles a crater draped in orchids and howler monkeys. Clouds roll in most afternoons, so mornings give the clearest views back down to Granada and the lake.

title: Swim the warm crater lake at Laguna de Apoyo
description: A volcanic crater lake warmed from below by geothermal vents, so it stays swimmable even when Nicaragua's other lakes turn cool. The clearest water and quietest docks are on the side facing away from the main road down from Masaya.

title: Walk barefoot across the white rooftop of Leon Cathedral
description: The largest cathedral in Central America, and a UNESCO site since 2011 - rangers hand out no footwear but do insist on covered shoulders before you climb to the roof's white domes. The poet Ruben Dario is buried at the foot of the altar, guarded by a stone lion.

title: Watch the Sunday pool crawl at San Juan del Sur
description: A fishing-village-turned-surf-town where the Christ of the Mercy statue on the headland is lit up every night and a weekly boat-bar crawl between beach clubs has become the main event for the backpacker crowd. The real surf beaches are a short taxi ride further up the coast, not the town beach itself.

title: Hike into the crater lagoon of Volcan Maderas
description: The quieter, wetter twin of Ometepe's two volcanoes, climbed through cloud forest thick with mud most of the year to a cold, dark crater lake at the top that most hikers only dip a foot into. Guides are compulsory and the round trip regularly takes eight hours.

title: Unplug on car-free Little Corn Island
description: No cars, no roads and until recently no reliable electricity after midnight - reached only by a small plane to Big Corn followed by an hour-long panga boat crossing that cancels outright in rough seas. The payoff is reef diving and empty beaches the mainland's Pacific coast lost years ago.

title: Tour a shade-grown coffee farm above Matagalpa
description: Nicaragua's coffee capital sits high enough in the hills that many farms still pick entirely by hand, and several now run their own tours through drying patios and roasting rooms. Visit outside the December-February harvest and you'll see the plants but not the picking.

title: Swim and jump the narrows of Somoto Canyon
description: A canyon only documented by geologists in 2004 despite locals having always known about it, now run with life jackets, short swims and cliff jumps of your choosing between towering rock walls. Afternoon storms in wet season can raise the water level fast, so guides push for a morning start.

title: Dive the reef wall off Roatan's West Bay
description: Part of the Mesoamerican Reef, the second-largest barrier reef system on earth, with a wall dive that drops from a few metres to open water within a short swim of the beach. Whale sharks pass offshore between March and April, though sightings are never guaranteed.

title: Snorkel the protected reef of Cayos Cochinos
description: Thirteen tiny cays and coral reef set aside as a protected marine reserve since the 1990s, with day-trip numbers capped and overnight stays limited to a single small research-linked eco-lodge. The endemic pink boa found on the islands lives nowhere else on earth.

title: Rappel down the face of Pulhapanzak Falls
description: A 43m curtain of water on the Rio Lindo that a local guide company rappels visitors down the rock beside, finishing in the spray at the base. The main viewing platform alone is worth the stop even skipping the rappel - it's one of the most photographed waterfalls in the country.

title: Bird-watch and drink craft beer at Lago de Yojoa
description: Honduras's only large natural lake and a stop for over 480 recorded bird species, ringed with cloud forest, coffee farms and - unexpectedly - the country's best-known microbrewery, which grew out of a hostel started by backpackers who never left.

title: Meet rescued macaws at Macaw Mountain
description: A rescue and breeding sanctuary a short tuk-tuk ride from the ruins, walking distance from Copan's own resident flock of wild scarlet macaws that roost around the archaeological park each evening. Entry doubles as support for the program that reintroduced macaws to the area after local extinction.

title: Eat Garifuna seafood on the beach at Tela
description: A Caribbean coast beach town with a strong Garifuna community, best known for pan de coco and fish stewed in coconut milk sold straight off beachfront grills. Punta dance performances happen most weekends in the Garifuna village of Triunfo de la Cruz just along the bay.

title: Hike the cloud forest trails of La Tigra
description: Honduras's first national park, a former silver-mining site reclaimed by cloud forest just 30 minutes from the capital's traffic. Quetzals turn up sometimes along the old mining trails between March and June, though the mist and mud year-round make for slow going regardless.

title: See the oldest working clock in the Americas at Comayagua
description: A colonial capital predating Tegucigalpa, whose cathedral holds a Moorish clock gifted by Spain's king in the 1600s and still keeping time today - older than any other clock still running on the continent. The town's Easter carpets of dyed sawdust rival Guatemala's more famous ones with a fraction of the crowds.

title: Hike to the turquoise crater lake of Santa Ana Volcano
description: El Salvador's highest volcano, climbed in a guided group as much for company as for terrain difficulty - the reward is a sulphurous turquoise crater lake that steams faintly at the edges. Starting early beats both the heat and the cloud that usually fills in by midday.

title: Wander the cobblestones of colonial Suchitoto
description: A whitewashed colonial town on the edge of Lake Suchitlan that was largely bypassed by the civil war's worst damage, which is why so much of its original architecture survived intact. Boat trips at dawn on the lake pass through wetlands thick with migratory birds.

title: Walk the buried Maya village at Joya de Ceren
description: Called the Pompeii of the Americas - a farming village buried intact under volcanic ash around 600AD, preserving everyday houses and kitchen gardens rather than the temples most Maya sites are built around. It's the only UNESCO site in the country and among the least visited anywhere in Central America.

title: Hike the rim of El Boqueron above San Salvador
description: A volcanic crater 5km across on the edge of the capital, with a smaller cone growing inside it from a 1917 eruption that buried nearby villages. The rim trail is an easy walk, and clear mornings give a full view over the entire Valle de las Hamacas below.

title: Swim the blue crater waters of Lago de Coatepeque
description: A collapsed-caldera lake so deep its centre has never been fully mapped, ringed with private docks and family-run lakeside restaurants rather than resorts. Weekday visits mean having whole stretches of shoreline to yourself; weekends bring half of San Salvador.

title: Learn to surf at Bitcoin Beach in El Zonte
description: A once-sleepy fishing beach nicknamed Bitcoin Beach after a 2019 experiment paid locals in crypto, which brought a wave of surf hostels and cafes without erasing the point break that made surfers stop here in the first place. Boards rent by the hour right off the black-sand beach.

title: Watch sunset from Havana's Malecon
description: An eight-kilometre seawall where the whole city gathers at dusk - fishermen, musicians, courting couples and vendors selling peanuts from paper cones. Big swells send spray clear across the road in winter, so watch the waves before you post up on the wall.

title: Swim the turquoise sands of Varadero
description: Twenty kilometres of white sand on a narrow peninsula, Cuba's best-resourced beach and the one built almost entirely for all-inclusive tourism rather than everyday Cuban life. For a more local feel, the town at the peninsula's western end still has independent paladares and casas particulares.

title: Snorkel the reef at the Bay of Pigs
description: The 1961 invasion site is now better known to divers than historians - a wall dive drops close to shore into some of the clearest water on the island, and the small museum in Playa Giron covers the failed landing in blunt, one-sided detail.

title: Spot the bee hummingbird in Zapata Swamp
description: The Caribbean's largest wetland and the only place on earth to see the bee hummingbird, the world's smallest bird, alongside Cuban crocodiles found nowhere else. Guides know the flowering trees the hummingbirds favour that week - go without one and you likely won't find either.

title: Walk the French colonial Prado in Cienfuegos
description: Founded by French settlers rather than the Spanish, which shows in the neoclassical Palacio de Valle and a grid of streets unusually wide for a Cuban colonial city. The rooftop bar at the Palacio serves the best sunset view over the bay for the price of one drink.

title: Follow live son music through Santiago de Cuba's Casas de la Trova
description: The birthplace of son and the spiritual home of Cuban carnival, hotter and less visited than Havana, with live music spilling out of the Casa de la Trova most nights without a cover charge. Late July's carnival is the loudest and largest in the country, and hotel rooms book out months ahead.

title: Visit the shrine of Cuba's patron saint at El Cobre
description: A basilica built on a former copper-mining town, holding a small black Virgin credited with miracles that pilgrims still walk to on their knees. The room behind the altar is lined with offerings left by everyone from desperate emigrants to Ernest Hemingway's Nobel medal, on loan for a time.

title: Summit Pico Turquino in the Sierra Maestra
description: Cuba's highest peak, reached by a two-day guided trek through the mountains where Fidel Castro's rebels hid out for two years before the revolution. A bust of Jose Marti sits at the summit, hauled up in pieces by the guerrillas themselves in 1957.

title: Eat cucurucho in Cuba's first colonial capital, Baracoa
description: Cut off from the rest of the island by mountains until a road finally connected it in 1965, which let a distinct cuisine survive - coconut, cacao and plantain dominate here in ways the rest of Cuba doesn't cook. Cucurucho, a cone of shredded coconut and fruit wrapped in a palm leaf, is sold on every corner.

title: Get lost in Camaguey's maze of colonial streets
description: Laid out deliberately as a labyrinth to confuse pirates rather than on the standard Spanish colonial grid, which still confuses GPS today. Giant clay tinajones that once caught rainwater sit outside houses across the city as an unofficial symbol of the place.

title: Pay respects at the Che Guevara Mausoleum in Santa Clara
description: Guevara's remains were returned from Bolivia and interred here in 1997, in the city he and his column famously captured by derailing an armoured train in 1958 - a restored section of that train sits as a memorial nearby. Bags and cameras are held at the door; photography inside the mausoleum itself is not allowed.

title: Beach-hop the resort cays of Cayo Coco
description: Connected to the mainland by a causeway built across the bay, which locals say altered water currents enough to change the fishing for years afterward. Flamingos gather in the shallows beside the causeway in numbers that rival anywhere else in the Caribbean.

title: Dive with silky sharks in Jardines de la Reina
description: A protected archipelago Cuba closed to fishing and left largely to scientists for decades, which is why the sharks here show almost no fear of divers. Access is only by liveaboard boat with a handful of licensed operators, and trips need booking most of a year ahead.

title: Hike to waterfalls in the Topes de Collantes mountains
description: A cloud forest reserve above Trinidad in the Escambray range, where trails drop to swimming holes like Salto del Caburni after a steep descent that's far harder coming back up. The old Soviet-built sanatorium at the entrance is now a hotel, and about the only accommodation inside the park.

title: Zipline over the reforested valley at Las Terrazas
description: A planned eco-community built in the 1970s to reforest land stripped bare by 19th-century coffee plantations, now Cuba's first biosphere reserve. The ruins of the old Buenavista coffee estate sit within walking distance of a zipline that crosses the artificial lake at the valley's centre.

title: Boat through the underground river at Cueva del Indio
description: A cave system used by escaped slaves as a hideout in the 19th century, toured on foot before the path gives way to a motorboat ride along the underground river that carved it. It sits a short ride from the tobacco-farm tours most visitors already build a Vinales day around.

title: Watch Afro-Cuban rumba at Callejon de Hamel
description: A single alley transformed by a local artist into a shrine to Santeria and Afro-Cuban identity, covered wall to wall in murals built from bathtubs and scrap metal. Sunday's rumba session draws a mixed crowd of neighbourhood regulars and travellers, and it starts whenever the drummers actually turn up.

title: Visit Bob Marley's birthplace and mausoleum at Nine Mile
description: The village where Marley was born, buried and is said to still visit in dreams according to the guides who grew up alongside him. His mausoleum room faces east, and shoes come off before the family will let you inside.

title: Watch the sunset over Seven Mile Beach in Negril
description: A near-uninterrupted stretch of white sand facing due west, which makes it one of the most reliable sunset-watching beaches in the Caribbean - beach bars post up speakers and rum-punch stands right at the water's edge for the nightly show.

title: Cliff jump at Rick's Cafe in Negril
description: Local jumpers dive from platforms up to 12m for tips before the crowd gets a turn from the lower ledges - the current can push you toward the rocks, so watch where the regulars enter before you jump. Arrive well before sunset; it's standing room only by the time the sky turns orange.

title: Swing into the pools at YS Falls
description: Seven tiers on private cattle-farm land, reached by a canopy-covered tractor ride from the car park rather than a hike. A rope swing off the second tier is the local rite of passage, though the falls are calm enough most of the year for anyone happy just to float.

title: Cruise for crocodiles on the Black River
description: Jamaica's longest river, stained the colour of tea by tannins from the swamp it drains rather than pollution, and home to the island's largest surviving population of American crocodiles. Boats leave from the town wharf and rangers know the same basking spots the crocodiles return to daily.

title: Bamboo raft the Rio Grande near Port Antonio
description: Errol Flynn is credited with turning the banana farmers' cargo rafts into a tourist ride in the 1950s after taking one downriver himself, and polers still steer 9m bamboo rafts the same slow three-hour route today. Go early - afternoon rain in the hills upstream can raise the current within the hour.

title: Tour the Trench Town Culture Yard
description: The government yard where Bob Marley, Peter Tosh and Bunny Wailer all lived before the Wailers existed, and where Marley wrote 'No Woman No Cry'. Guides here mostly grew up in Trench Town themselves, and the tour funds a still-active community music program.

title: Swim the mineral waters of Doctor's Cave Beach
description: A doctor promoted the beach's waters as therapeutic in the 1920s, kicking off Montego Bay's whole run as a health resort - the mineral claims didn't hold up, but the calm, clear bay he chose still explains why the area became a resort strip in the first place.

title: Tour Jamaica's oldest rum distillery at Appleton Estate
description: Distilling continuously since 1749 in the Nassau Valley, where the limestone-filtered river water and volcanic soil are the estate's whole pitch for why its rum tastes different from anywhere else. The tasting at the end includes vintages not sold outside the estate itself.

title: Wander the ironwork balconies of Jacmel
description: A 19th-century coffee-export port whose merchants imported cast iron from France for the balconies that still define the town, and whose Carnival papier-mache masks are considered the most inventive in the country. Regarded as one of the calmer parts of Haiti to visit, though conditions nationwide change quickly and should be checked immediately before any trip.

title: Swim the turquoise tiered pools of Bassin Bleu
description: Three linked pools reached by a scramble down rock and a rope-assisted final descent, fed by an underground spring that keeps the water an improbable blue-green year-round. Local guides are compulsory and effectively necessary for the descent itself, not just for directions.

title: Explore the ruined royal palace of Sans-Souci
description: Built by King Henri Christophe as his Versailles, then wrecked by an 1842 earthquake and never rebuilt - the roofless shell of the throne room and royal apartments still shows the scale he intended. It sits at the base of the mountain the Citadelle crowns, and most visitors see both on the one trip.

title: Reach the car-free beaches of Ile-a-Vache by boat
description: A small island off Les Cayes with no cars and barely any roads, reached only by a short boat crossing. Its calmer south-coast setting has kept it further from the unrest affecting travel to much of the mainland, though independent verification of current conditions is essential before going.

title: Swim the horseshoe bay at Flamenco Beach
description: Regularly ranked among the best beaches in the world, with two rusting tanks left on the sand from a decommissioned US Navy bombing range - swimming near them is discouraged but nobody stops you looking. The only way in is a 20-minute ferry from the main island, so day-trippers race the last boat back.

title: Watch wild paso fino horses roam Vieques' beaches
description: Descendants of Spanish colonial stock left to run free after the US Navy vacated its bombing range in 2003, now grazing unfenced on Sun Bay and along the island's back roads. Former base land makes up most of the island's protected wildlife refuge today, one of the odder legacies of a military withdrawal anywhere.

title: Ride the red fire truck at Ponce's Parque de Bombas
description: A red-and-black striped 1882 firehouse turned museum in the plaza of Puerto Rico's second city, still the most photographed building on the south coast. The Museum of Art nearby holds the island's best pre-modern European collection, a legacy of the sugar and rum money that built the city's mansions.

title: Ride into the Rio Camuy cave system
description: One of the largest cave networks in the western hemisphere, carved by the third-largest underground river on earth - a trolley takes you down into the sinkhole entrance before the walking tour starts. Book the first tour of the day in high season; tickets are timed and sell out by early afternoon.

title: Frame the Rio Grande de Arecibo valley from Cueva Ventana
description: A natural window cut into a limestone cliff by centuries of water, framing one of the most photographed views on the island. It's a guided tour on private land rather than a free lookout, and closed-toe shoes are enforced at the entrance.

title: Eat along the Pork Highway in Guavate
description: A strip of roadside lechoneras in the mountains outside Cayey, each roasting whole pigs over charcoal pits out back - weekends bring live music and traffic jams of Puerto Ricans driving up just for lunch. Order by pointing at the pig rather than reading a menu; most places don't have one.

title: Kayak the glowing water of Laguna Grande
description: A mangrove-fringed bioluminescent bay reached only by kayak through a narrow channel from the ocean, dimmer than Vieques' Mosquito Bay but far easier to combine with a day based in San Juan. Moonless nights are non-negotiable - even a half-moon washes the glow out almost completely.

title: Fly a kite on the ramparts of El Morro
description: A 16th-century fort guarding San Juan's harbour mouth, with lawns on top so broad and windswept that flying a kite there has become as much a local tradition as the history tour itself. The sentry boxes at the corners, called garitas, are recognised enough to appear on Puerto Rico's own coat of arms.

title: Surf the winter swells at Rincon
description: The west coast town that put Puerto Rico on the surfing map after hosting the 1968 World Surfing Championships, with a lighthouse park still the best spot to watch humpback whales pass offshore in the same winter months the swell peaks.

title: Snorkel the mangrove cay locals call Gilligan's Island
description: A small nature reserve cay off the dry southwest coast, reachable only by a short public ferry from Guanica rather than a tour boat - a deliberately low-key contrast to San Juan's cruise-ship crowds. Bring your own snorkel gear and lunch; there are no vendors on the cay itself.

title: Walk the oldest streets in the Americas in Zona Colonial
description: Santo Domingo's colonial core, the first permanent European settlement in the Americas, with the continent's first cathedral, first paved street and first university all within a few blocks. Calle El Conde gets loud and touristy after dark; the streets one block over stay quiet enough to feel the age of the place.

title: Climb and jump the 27 Waterfalls of Damajagua
description: A river canyon of stacked waterfalls climbed by ladder and rope before you jump or slide down each one on the way back - guides make the whole route compulsory, and stopping short of a jump you don't like is completely normal. Most trips stop around the twelfth fall; reaching all 27 is a longer, harder day.

title: Swim the cenote at Hoyo Azul
description: A turquoise freshwater sinkhole inside the Scape Park reserve, reached by an off-road buggy or zipline rather than a footpath. It sits on private resort land, so access is ticketed even though it looks like a wild spot dropped in the middle of the jungle.

title: Walk the white sand of Bavaro Beach
description: The stretch of coast that built Punta Cana's all-inclusive industry, with a reef offshore calm enough that the beach rarely gets the rough shore break found elsewhere on the east coast. Public access points between the resorts still let non-guests walk the sand for free.

title: Summit Pico Duarte, the Caribbean's highest peak
description: A multi-day trek with mules to carry gear, through pine forest that gets cold enough at altitude for frost most mornings - a genuine surprise in a Caribbean country. Permits and a licensed guide are compulsory and arranged through the parks agency in Jarabacoa before you start.

title: Boat through the mogotes and mangroves of Los Haitises
description: Limestone karst domes rising straight out of mangrove swamp and bay, dotted with Taino cave paintings reachable only by the same small boats that wind through the mangrove channels. Morning trips beat both the heat and the afternoon chop that can cancel crossings from Samana.

title: Day-trip the palm-lined sand of Isla Saona
description: A national park island reached by catamaran or speedboat through a shallow natural pool where the boats stop so everyone can wade waist-deep with starfish underfoot. It's one of the most-sold excursions out of Punta Cana, so an early boat is the only real way to beat the crowds.

title: Kitesurf the trade winds at Cabarete
description: Steady onshore trade winds and a reef-protected bay made this stretch of the north coast one of the world's kitesurfing capitals, with schools lined up along the beach happy to take total beginners. Afternoon winds are the most reliable; mornings are usually too calm to launch.

title: Stand behind the curtain of Salto de Jimenoa
description: A waterfall in the mountain town best known as the country's whitewater and canyoning base, with a swinging bridge over the gorge and a viewing platform tucked directly behind the falling water. The same river below town runs some of the best rafting in the Caribbean during wet season.

title: Spot crocodiles on Lago Enriquillo, the Caribbean's lowest point
description: A hypersaline lake below sea level, home to the largest population of American crocodiles in the Caribbean and an island within it, Isla Cabritos, reachable only by park boat. The lake's level has risen and fallen dramatically over the past two decades, swallowing roads and forcing the park's own entrance to move.

title: Swim with the pigs of Big Major Cay
description: Nobody agrees on how feral pigs ended up on an uninhabited cay, but they now swim out to greet every boat that anchors offshore expecting food. Feed them only what your boat operator provides - bread and the wrong scraps have made pigs sick enough that some have died in past years.

title: Snorkel the sunlit cavern of Thunderball Grotto
description: A hollow limestone rock with underwater entrances and a skylight open to the sky, named for the James Bond film shot inside it and used again in two later Bond movies. The cave floods at high tide, so trips are timed to a window either side of low tide when you can swim in without ducking underwater.

title: Free dive Dean's Blue Hole
description: The second-deepest known saltwater blue hole on earth at over 200m, dropping off a few metres from an otherwise ordinary-looking beach - it's hosted world championship freediving events for exactly that reason. Snorkelling the rim needs no experience at all; the drop-off just happens to be there.

title: Climb the Queen's Staircase in Nassau
description: Sixty-six limestone steps hand-carved by enslaved labourers in the 1790s, one for each year of Queen Victoria's reign by the time it was named for her decades later. Junkanoo, the country's signature street parade, takes over Bay Street before dawn every Boxing Day and New Year's Day.

title: Ride the water slides at Atlantis Paradise Island
description: A resort built around a fictional lost-city theme, with a slide that drops riders through a clear tube inside a shark-filled lagoon. Non-guests can buy a day pass to the water park, usually the cheaper way in compared with booking a room.

title: Walk the pink sand of Harbour Island
description: Three miles of sand tinted pink by crushed coral and shell fragments mixed through the white sand, best seen in the low light of early morning or late afternoon when the colour is most obvious. Golf carts are the main transport on the island; rental cars are barely used at all.

title: Swim with wild dolphins off Bimini
description: A resident pod of Atlantic spotted dolphins in the shallow banks off Bimini has interacted with boats for decades, closely enough that operators run dedicated wild-encounter trips rather than a captive pool. Hemingway used the island as a fishing base in the 1930s, and the marina bar he drank in is still open.

title: Kayak one of the world's longest underwater cave systems at Lucayan
description: Over 10km of mapped underwater passages beneath the park, among the longest charted anywhere, though only two chambers are open for the public to walk or swim into unassisted. A boardwalk through the pine forest and mangrove above ends at Gold Rock Beach, used as a filming location for a Pirates of the Caribbean sequel.

title: Kayak the neon lagoon of Chalk Sound
description: A shallow national park lagoon studded with dozens of tiny rock islets, coloured an almost artificial turquoise by a floor of white marl sand under very shallow water. Sunset paddles catch the colour at its most saturated, right as the wind usually drops for the evening.

title: Snorkel the wall drop-off at Grand Turk
description: The barrier reef here sits just a few hundred metres offshore before plunging over 2,000m down a near-vertical wall, one of the closest deep-water drop-offs to any beach in the Caribbean. Humpback whales pass close enough between January and March to be seen from shore on a calm day.

title: Explore the limestone chambers of Conch Bar Caves
description: The largest cave system in the Bahamas archipelago chain, with bat colonies, underground pools and Lucayan artefacts left behind by the islands' first inhabitants. There's no visitor centre or lighting - a local guide with a flashlight is effectively required to see past the entrance chamber.

title: Eat conch at the Thursday night fish fry
description: A weekly street party at Bight Park where home cooks grill conch, fish and ribs and a local band plays rake-and-scrape, the islands' homegrown genre built around a handsaw played like an instrument. It's as much a resident night out as a tourist stop, and it only happens on Thursdays.

title: Watch the Atlantic pound the boulders at Bathsheba
description: Giant mushroom-shaped rocks carved by wave action on the rugged east coast, and the annual venue for the Soup Bowl surf contest even though the current here is too strong for casual swimming. The Andromeda Botanic Gardens sit just above the beach if the surf keeps you out of the water.

title: Tour the world's oldest rum distillery at Mount Gay
description: Distilling since 1703, with paperwork to prove it - the oldest continuously dated rum brand anywhere. The tasting flight at the end runs from the entry-level mixing rum up to bottles that never leave the island's duty-free shelves.

title: Swim a tidal pool inside Animal Flower Cave
description: A sea cave at the island's northern tip named for the sea anemones once found in its pools, with a swimmable rock pool that opens straight onto Atlantic swells crashing just outside. Rough seas close the lower cave entirely, so a calm-day forecast is worth checking before the drive out.

title: Eat flying fish at the Oistins Fish Fry
description: A Friday-night fixture where fishing-village grills turn out flying fish and mahi-mahi to a soundtrack of soca and a crowd that's equal parts tourists and Bajans out for the weekend. Arrive hungry before 7pm - the best stalls sell out before the music really gets going.

title: Walk among free-roaming green monkeys at the Wildlife Reserve
description: A mahogany forest reserve with no cages between you and the green monkeys, red-footed tortoises and peacocks that wander it freely - the monkeys descend from a small troop first brought over from West Africa centuries ago. Feeding time around midday is the most reliable moment to see the monkeys up close.

title: Jump up at Crop Over, Barbados' answer to Carnival
description: Rooted in the historic end-of-sugar-harvest celebrations enslaved workers once held when the cane was finally cut, now a months-long festival building to the Grand Kadooment parade every August. Costume bands sell out early; joining one needs booking months ahead of the actual parade day.

title: Walk the surface of the Pitch Lake
description: The largest natural deposit of asphalt on earth, still slowly bubbling and swallowing anything left on it too long - guides point out tools and even a small crane the lake has claimed over the decades. It supplied the asphalt for London's streets over a century ago and is still mined today.

title: Watch scarlet ibis flood home to roost at Caroni Swamp
description: The country's national bird returns to the mangroves in flocks thousands strong right at sunset, turning whole trees red in the last light. Boats leave at low tide only, timed so the outgoing water helps push you back out through the narrow channels afterward.

title: Eat bake and shark on Maracas Bay
description: A palm-backed beach over the mountains from Port of Spain, famous less for the swimming than for the fried-shark sandwiches sold from a row of stalls right on the sand - Richard's is the most famous, but locals argue endlessly over which stall does it best.

title: Wade the sandbar at the Nylon Pool
description: A waist-deep sandbar in open water off Buccoo Reef, named by Princess Margaret in the 1960s for how clear the water looked against her nylon stockings. Boat tours anchor here as a swim stop on the way to or from snorkelling the reef itself.

title: Climb the three tiers of Argyle Waterfall
description: Tobago's tallest waterfall, reached by a short rainforest walk with a local guide required at the entrance gate. Each of the three pools is deep enough to swim, and the top tier is quiet enough most mornings that you may have it to yourself before the tour buses arrive.

title: Watch leatherback turtles nest at Grande Riviere
description: One of the highest-density leatherback nesting beaches on earth relative to its size, with females hauling out most nights in season to dig nests the size of a bathtub. Licensed guides with red-filtered lights are compulsory after dark - white light and flash photography can disorient nesting turtles.

title: Snorkel straight off the sand at Anse Chastanet
description: The reef starts just a few strokes from the shoreline, dropping quickly enough into deeper water that both snorkellers and certified divers use the same entry point. It's one of the only reefs on the island's west coast walkable directly from a public beach rather than a boat.

title: Climb the near-vertical Petit Piton
description: The steeper and more technical of the two Pitons, with sections of rope and rebar bolted into the rock face near the top - guides can and do turn back clients who aren't coping. Gros Piton next door is the easier climb of the pair if the exposure here sounds like too much.

title: Sail into the palm-ringed harbour of Marigot Bay
description: A natural harbour so enclosed by hills that a British admiral once hid his fleet here under cut palm branches to fool a pursuing French squadron. A small pedestrian ferry still shuttles across the narrow channel instead of a bridge, keeping the resort side properly cut off from the road.

title: Soak in the mineral baths below Diamond Falls
description: The waterfall runs mineral-streaked shades of yellow and grey off the same volcanic vents that feed Sulphur Springs nearby, through botanical gardens planted originally for Louis XVI's troops. The mineral baths were commissioned in the 1780s and are still fed from the same hot spring today.

title: Eat street-grilled seafood at the Anse La Raye Fish Fry
description: A Friday-night village street party far less geared to cruise-ship crowds than the bigger tourist-strip fish fries elsewhere on the island, with grills set up right along the main street selling whatever the day's catch was. Cash only, and stalls sell out early once the fishing boats have had a lean week.

title: Snorkel the volcanic bubbles of Champagne Reef
description: Geothermal vents on the seafloor release a steady stream of warm bubbles that make the water fizz around you like the reef's namesake drink. It's an easy shore entry rather than a boat dive, which makes it one of the most accessible volcanic snorkel sites anywhere in the Caribbean.

title: View the twin cascades of Trafalgar Falls
description: Locally nicknamed Father and Mother Falls for their contrasting size and force, visible together from one viewing platform reached by an easy ten-minute walk. Getting to the pool at Father Falls' base requires a scramble over slick volcanic boulders that's rougher than the approach walk suggests.

title: Swim the narrow volcanic walls of Titou Gorge
description: A slot canyon carved by the Breakfast River, swum rather than walked for most of its length between sheer black volcanic rock. A Pirates of the Caribbean sequel filmed a key scene here, and the gorge narrows enough in places that you can touch both walls at once.

title: Learn canoe-building in the Kalinago Territory
description: Home to the largest remaining population of pre-Columbian Kalinago people in the Caribbean, on land guaranteed by an 1903 agreement with the British. Artisans still hollow out gommier canoes by hand and demonstrate cassava bread making the same way their grandparents did.

title: Hike through rainforest to Middleham Falls
description: A 90m drop inside Morne Trois Pitons National Park, reached by a muddy, root-tangled trail that crosses the same river twice before the falls come into view. The pool at the base stays cold year-round, fed straight off the mountain rather than warmed by any lowland run.

title: Walk the two miles of sand at Grand Anse Beach
description: Grenada's best-known beach and the one most of the island's resorts are built along, but the sand stays wide and uncrowded enough that a two-mile walk end to end rarely feels busy outside cruise-ship days. Vendors sell nutmeg-spiced everything from ice cream to rum punch right on the sand.

title: See a water wheel still crushing cane at River Antoine
description: The Caribbean's oldest functioning water-powered distillery, running on the same 18th-century wheel and vats since 1785 with barely a modern part in sight. The rum produced here is bottled at a strength high enough that it's restricted from being carried on some flights.

title: Tour a working nutmeg station in Gouyave
description: Grenada supplies a large share of the world's nutmeg, and this processing station has sorted, dried and graded it by hand since the 1950s - the same building survived being flattened by a hurricane and rebuilt around the same machinery. Friday night's Fish Friday street festival in the same town is the better-known reason people already plan to be in Gouyave.

title: Hike between the three tiers of Concord Falls
description: The lowest fall is a five-minute walk from the car park and swimmable by anyone; reaching the upper two tiers means another 30 minutes of steep, often slippery trail where a guide is worth having for the crossing points. Locals use the lowest pool as an actual swimming hole, not just a photo stop.

title: Island-hop to Carriacou for its regatta culture
description: Grenada's sister island, still building traditional wooden sloops by eye rather than blueprint in the town of Windward, a skill descended directly from Scottish shipwrights who settled here generations ago. The annual Carriacou Regatta races those same boats and turns the whole island into a long weekend party.

title: Boat into the world's largest frigatebird colony on Barbuda
description: Codrington Lagoon holds the largest nesting colony of magnificent frigatebirds in the Western Hemisphere, with males inflating a red throat pouch the size of a balloon to attract mates each mating season. Access is by shallow-draft boat only, and the colony is at its most active between September and April.

title: Walk eleven miles of empty pink sand on Barbuda
description: Crushed coral gives the sand a faint pink tinge along a beach so long and undeveloped that you can walk for hours without passing another building. A 2017 hurricane forced a full evacuation of the island, and much of Barbuda's coastline still sees a fraction of Antigua's visitor numbers.

title: Catch the Sunday sunset party at Shirley Heights
description: A former military lookout above English Harbour with a clear view down over Nelson's Dockyard and the yachts anchored below, now known island-wide for its Sunday-evening barbecue and steel-pan session timed to the sunset. Arrive by mid-afternoon - the car park fills early once the music starts.

title: Watch waves blast through Devil's Bridge's blowholes
description: A natural limestone arch on the exposed Atlantic coast, carved by centuries of wave action into blowholes that shoot spray metres into the air on a rough day. Legend holds enslaved people threw themselves off it rather than face recapture, which is where the name comes from.

title: Bodysurf the crescent swell at Half Moon Bay
description: One of the more exposed of Antigua's 365 beaches, with a crescent of sand facing straight into the Atlantic swell that makes it better for bodysurfing than the calm leeward beaches most resorts sit on. There's no real development along it, so bring your own shade and water.

title: Walk the ramparts of Brimstone Hill Fortress
description: Built by enslaved African labourers over a century for the British, earning the nickname the Gibraltar of the West Indies for how it commanded the surrounding sea. On a clear day the view from the top takes in five or six neighbouring islands at once.

title: Ride the last railway in the West Indies
description: A narrow-gauge line built to haul sugar cane to Basseterre, repurposed since the industry's 2005 collapse into a double-decker sightseeing train that circles most of the island's coast. The upper open-air deck gets the better view; the lower car has the bar.

title: Hike into the crater of Mount Liamuiga
description: A dormant volcano whose crater rim trail ends at a viewpoint looking down into a crater filled with cloud forest rather than lava. The final approach is a steep, rope-assisted scramble through mud that makes the round trip a full day even though the distance looks short on a map.

title: Scramble to the cloud forest summit of Nevis Peak
description: Steeper than it looks from the coast, with ropes fixed to tree roots for the final push through a forest thick enough that the summit itself has almost no view. Most guides rate it harder than its modest 985m suggests, purely because of how relentlessly steep the trail is.

title: Watch the sunset over Pinney's Beach
description: A four-mile stretch of dark volcanic-gold sand facing west across the Caribbean Sea toward Saint Kitts' own volcano, quiet enough outside the handful of beach bars that most of it stays empty even in high season. It's a short walk from Charlestown, Nevis' compact Georgian-era capital.

title: Snorkel the reef lagoon of the Tobago Cays
description: Five uninhabited islets ringed by Horseshoe Reef, which breaks the swell enough to create a calm turquoise lagoon that's one of the most sailed-to anchorages in the Caribbean. Green turtles graze the seagrass beds right beside the main snorkel mooring, used to boat traffic after decades as a marine park.

title: Learn model boat-building in Port Elizabeth, Bequia
description: A whaling and boat-building tradition survives here that's mostly vanished elsewhere in the Caribbean, with artisans still crafting museum-quality miniature schooners by hand in small waterfront workshops. Bequia still holds a small annual whaling quota under an aboriginal-subsistence exemption, one of the last such allowances in the Western hemisphere.

title: Day-trip the private island of Mustique
description: A privately managed island of celebrity holiday homes with no casual walk-in access - day visitors arrive by charter boat or plane and stick to Macaroni Beach and Basil's Bar rather than the residential side. It's one of the only Grenadine islands where turning up on a public ferry simply isn't an option.

title: Hike La Soufriere after its 2021 eruption
description: The volcano that forced a full evacuation of northern Saint Vincent in April 2021 reopened its trail once ash settled, and the summit crater now looks markedly different to older photos online after the eruption reshaped it. Check locally before setting out - access still closes on short notice if activity picks up.

title: Boat to the remote Falls of Baleine
description: A 20m waterfall on the island's roadless northwest coast, reachable only by boat since no road ever reached this stretch of shoreline. The short walk in from the landing crosses the same river three times before the falls come into view.

title: Reach the volcanic-rock Natural Pool by 4WD
description: A saltwater pool enclosed by volcanic rock on Arikok's wild windward coast, reachable only by 4WD, ATV, horseback or a long hike since no paved road gets close. Big swells send waves right over the rock walls, so check conditions before jumping in.

title: Photograph the divi-divi trees on Eagle Beach
description: Constant trade winds have permanently bent the island's divi-divi trees to point southwest, and the handful growing right on this beach have become the most photographed trees in Aruba. The beach itself is wide enough and quiet enough that it regularly outranks its busier neighbour, Palm Beach, in traveller polls.

title: Snorkel the calm shallows of Baby Beach
description: A horseshoe-shaped lagoon at the island's southern tip, sheltered enough by its reef that the water rarely gets above waist-deep for a long way out - built for exactly the young kids its name suggests. It sits beside an old oil refinery, an odd backdrop to one of the calmest swimming spots on the island.

title: Watch sunset from the California Lighthouse dunes
description: Named for the SS California, a steamship wrecked nearby in 1891, standing over wind-sculpted dunes on the island's undeveloped northwest tip. The restaurant beside it is a better bet for the view than the lighthouse interior, which keeps irregular opening hours.

title: Explore the crumbling Bushiribana Gold Mill Ruins
description: Stone walls of an 1872 gold-smelting operation left to erode on the wild north coast, a reminder that Aruba ran a real gold rush decades before tourism existed. There's no fence, ticket booth or set path - just the ruins, the surf beyond them, and a scatter of balanced rock cairns other visitors have left behind.

title: Photograph the pastel waterfront of Willemstad
description: Dutch colonial merchant houses painted in candy colours line the Handelskade, reputedly because a 19th-century governor with migraines decided plain white walls glared too much in the sun and had them all repainted. The Queen Emma pontoon bridge across the channel swings open constantly for ship traffic, so budget extra time if you need to cross.

title: Summit Curacao's highest point in Christoffel National Park
description: A scramble up loose volcanic rock to the island's high point at 375m, best started before 8am since the exposed final push turns brutal once the sun is properly up. The reward from the top is a full view across Curacao's dry, cactus-studded interior to the sea on both sides.

title: Snorkel the coral wall at Playa Kenepa
description: A cove ringed by low cliffs where the reef starts just metres from the sand and drops into deeper water fast, drawing a heavier local crowd on weekends than the island's north-shore resort beaches. Its twin cove next door, Kenepa Chikitu, is quieter and reached by a short cliff-top walk.

title: Tour the limestone chambers of Hato Caves
description: Coral limestone caves formed when the whole area was still a reef beneath the sea, now home to a colony of long-nosed bats that roost in the ceiling during the day. Guided tours are the only way in, timed through chambers with names like the Cathedral for their scale.

title: Taste the original blue curacao at the Senior distillery
description: Made from the dried peel of the laraha citrus, a bitter local orange that grows almost nowhere but Curacao's dry soil after being abandoned as inedible centuries ago. The blue colour is a 20th-century marketing addition - the original triple-sec version has no colour at all and is what the family recipe actually tastes like.

title: Watch waves explode through Shete Boka's blowholes
description: A wild north-coast park named for its seven inlets, where Atlantic swell forces water through collapsed cave roofs called bokas with enough force to soak onlookers standing well back. Boka Tabla's cave floor can be walked into during calm seas, right below the crashing surf overhead.

title: Walk the powder sand of Seven Mile Beach
description: Closer to six miles by most surveys, but it's stayed the name regardless - a public beach law here keeps every stretch behind the resorts open to anyone, unlike many Caribbean islands where hotels wall off their frontage. Sunset cocktails at a beach bar are as much the local ritual as the swimming.

title: Hold a green sea turtle at the Cayman Turtle Centre
description: Founded originally as a commercial turtle farm, now split between conservation, education and a lagoon where visitors can handle young turtles under supervision. It's controversial among some conservationists for that mixed history, worth knowing before you decide whether to visit.

title: Kayak the glowing water of Grand Cayman's bio bay
description: Dinoflagellates in the mangrove-fringed bay light up electric blue with every paddle stroke on a moonless night, dimmer than it was a decade ago after boat traffic and shoreline lighting took a toll, so operators now cap group sizes and ban swimming to help it recover.

title: Dive the sheer drop of Bloody Bay Wall
description: A reef wall that starts in shallow water just off the beach and plunges to over 1,000m within a few hundred metres, rated among the best wall dives on earth by generations of dive magazines. Little Cayman itself has no traffic lights and fewer than 200 permanent residents, so the wall sees a fraction of Grand Cayman's dive traffic.

title: Spot flamingos and eat lobster on Anegada
description: A flat coral atoll unlike the volcanic peaks of the rest of the BVI, ringed by the fourth-largest barrier reef on earth and home to a flock of reintroduced flamingos in its salt ponds. Its lobster is grilled at a handful of beach shacks that between them define the entire tourist economy of the island.

title: Drink a Painkiller at the beach bar that invented it
description: The Soggy Dollar Bar earned its name because there was no dock for years, so everyone swam ashore with wet cash to pay for the rum cocktail it made famous. Yachts anchor two and three deep off White Bay by afternoon, most of them having sailed over just for this beach.

title: Hike the rainforest summit of Sage Mountain
description: The BVI's highest point at 521m, protected as the territory's first national park specifically to save a pocket of rainforest found nowhere else on Tortola's otherwise dry hillsides. The summit view takes in a chain of surrounding islands, weather depending, with almost no other hikers on the trail most days.

title: Snorkel the pirate caves off Norman Island
description: Said to be the real-world inspiration for Treasure Island, with sea caves along its shore that sailors have long claimed once hid pirate loot. The Willy T, a floating bar anchored in the bay, is the usual finish for a snorkel trip, complete with a rope swing off the top deck.

title: Swim the calm horseshoe of Magens Bay
description: A mile of protected, near-wave-free sand regularly named among the world's best beaches, kept undeveloped by a 1946 trust that donated the land to the territory for exactly that purpose. It fills up fast when a cruise ship is in port, so mornings before 10am are the quietest window.

title: Follow the underwater snorkel trail at Buck Island
description: A national monument reef with a marked underwater trail installed by the National Park Service so snorkellers can follow signposts identifying coral and fish without a guide. Boats to the island leave from Christiansted, and landing is only permitted on the beach side, not the reef itself.

title: Island-hop into Cruz Bay by ferry
description: St John's only real town and the arrival point for the ferry from St Thomas, small enough to walk end to end in fifteen minutes but with more than two-thirds of the island behind it protected as national park. Skinny Legs and the other harbourside bars are the standard first and last stop of any trip here.

title: Walk the underwater observatory at Coral World
description: An offshore tower with windows sunk 15 feet below the surface, giving a fish's-eye view of the reef without getting wet, alongside a semi-submarine tour and a shark encounter pool for the braver visitors. It sits right next to Coki Beach, one of the better shore-snorkelling spots on the island if the aquarium isn't enough.

title: Cross the pontoon bridge inside Crystal Caves
description: Discovered in 1907 by two boys chasing a lost cricket ball, dropping 120 feet down to a lake so clear the floor is visible through water that looks only a few feet deep. A floating pontoon bridge crosses the lake itself, timed on a tour rather than open for wandering alone.

title: Walk the pink sand crescent of Horseshoe Bay
description: Crushed red foraminifera shells mixed through the white sand give Bermuda's beaches their pink tinge, most visible in the wet sand right at the waterline rather than higher up the beach. A rock arch at the far end shelters a smaller, quieter cove if the main bay gets crowded with cruise-day visitors.

title: Walk the oldest English town in the New World
description: Continuously settled since 1612 and a UNESCO World Heritage site for it, with a street plan still following the original colonial layout rather than any later redesign. Tourists get 'ducked' in a re-enactment of the town's old punishment stool most weeks in season, dunked into the harbour to laughs rather than punishment now.

title: Explore the fortress walls of the Royal Naval Dockyard
description: Built by enslaved and convict labour over decades to guard the western approach to Bermuda for the British fleet, now the cruise-ship port and home to the National Museum inside the old Keep. Snorkel Park Beach, built into the old dockyard moat, is one of the few Bermuda beaches with a bar right on the sand.

title: Climb Gibbs Hill Lighthouse for a 360-degree island view
description: One of the first cast-iron lighthouses ever built, prefabricated in England and shipped out in pieces in 1846, still guiding ships with its original Fresnel-style optic. The 185 spiral steps to the top are the only way up - there's no lift, and the walkway outside catches more wind than the climb prepares you for.

title: Dive Bermuda's ring of shipwrecks
description: More recorded shipwrecks per square mile than almost anywhere on earth, wrecked over centuries on the reef that rings the island - some sit in under 20 feet of water, shallow enough for snorkellers to see hull timbers without diving gear at all. The reef that sank all those ships is the same one that now protects the wrecks from ocean swell.

title: Wander the harbourfront in Bermuda's capital, Hamilton
description: A capital small enough to cross on foot in twenty minutes, with pastel storefronts and businessmen still turning out in tailored Bermuda shorts and knee socks as standard office wear. The ferry across the harbour to Dockyard is a cheaper and better view than any bus.
